Information received since the FOMC met in May points to continued labor-market strength and moderate growth, a combination that rule-based frameworks (e.g., Taylor-type rules and the Clarida–Galí–Gertler reaction function) typically interpret as warranting gradual policy normalization even with inflation running somewhat below 2%. The Committee’s emphasis on a symmetric 2% objective and anchored expectations is consistent with inflation-forecast targeting principles (Svensson and Woodford), while the acknowledgment that market-based inflation compensation remains low fits evidence that term premia can depress breakevens independently of expected inflation (Cochrane–Piazzesi). The plan to begin balance-sheet normalization while maintaining an accommodative stance, alongside continued reinvestments and IOER-based implementation, aligns with post-2008 operating guidance (Goodfriend) and the literature’s support for interest-rate smoothing to limit real-side volatility, including cost-channel effects on firms’ working capital (Christiano–Eichenbaum–Evans; Ravenna–Walsh). Overall, the tone is cautiously optimistic—solid labor conditions and ongoing investment with balanced risks, tempered by below-target inflation—yielding a mildly positive assessment.
